title: Longest Common Subsequence
problem_statement:
Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. If there is no common subsequence, return 0.

A subsequence of a string is a new string generated from the original string with some characters (can be none) deleted without changing the relative order of the remaining characters.

For example, "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde".
A common subsequence of two strings is a subsequence that is common to both strings.
output_format: An integer representing the length of the longest common subsequence
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace" and its length is 3.
The longest common subsequence is "abc" and its length is 3.
There is no common subsequence, so the result is 0.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.approach: Explore all possible subsequences recursively by comparing characters at each position.
solutions.description: Use recursion to explore all possibilities: if characters match, include them and move forward in both strings; otherwise, try advancing in either string and take the maximum.

explanation.overview: This recursive solution explores all possible subsequences by comparing characters at each position and making decisions based on whether they match.

step_by_step.step_1: Start with both indices at position 0
step_by_step.step_2: Check if either string has been fully traversed (base case)
step_by_step.step_3: If characters match, include them in the subsequence and move both indices forward
step_by_step.step_4: If characters don't match, try two options: advance first string or advance second string
step_by_step.step_5: Take the maximum of the two options
step_by_step.step_6: Return the longest common subsequence length

explanation.why_it_works: The algorithm works by exploring all possible ways to form subsequences from both strings. When characters match, they must be part of the optimal solution for that branch. When they don't match, we explore both possibilities (skip character in text1 or skip in text2) and take the maximum, ensuring we find the longest common subsequence.
explanation.when_to_use: Use this approach for understanding the problem fundamentals or when inputs are very small. It demonstrates the recursive nature of the problem but is impractical for larger inputs due to exponential time complexity.
invariants: At each recursive call, i and j represent valid positions in their respective strings or equal the string length
The function returns the length of the longest common subsequence starting from positions i and j
All possible subsequences are explored through the recursive tree

explanation.why_it_works: Memoization works because the problem has overlapping subproblems. Many different paths in the recursive tree lead to the same (i, j) state. By caching results, we ensure each unique state is computed only once, converting an exponential algorithm into a polynomial one.

solutions.description: Create a 2D DP table where dp[i][j] represents the LCS length for text1[i:] and text2[j:]. Fill the table from bottom-right to top-left.

explanation.overview: This bottom-up approach builds a complete 2D table where each cell represents the LCS length for the remaining substrings. It processes the strings from end to beginning, ensuring all dependencies are computed before they're needed.

step_by_step.step_4: If characters don't match, take the maximum of advancing in either string

step_by_step.step_6: The answer is in dp[0][0], representing the full strings

explanation.why_it_works: The table approach works by building solutions from smaller subproblems. Each cell dp[i][j] correctly represents the LCS length for text1[i:] and text2[j:] because it either includes matching characters (diagonal + 1) or takes the best result from skipping one character (max of adjacent cells).
explanation.when_to_use: Use this approach when you need to solve all subproblems anyway, prefer iterative solutions, or want to reconstruct the actual LCS (not just its length). It's more intuitive for many people than recursion.

explanation.why_it_works: The algorithm works because each row only depends on the row below it. By processing from bottom to top and maintaining just two rows, we preserve all necessary information while using linear space instead of quadratic.
explanation.when_to_use: Use this approach when space is limited and you're processing large strings. It maintains O(m*n) time complexity while significantly reducing memory usage.

explanation.overview: This is the most space-efficient solution, using only one array and a temporary variable. The key insight is that we can update the array in-place while using 'prev' to remember the diagonal value that would have been in the second array.

step_by_step.step_1: Swap strings to ensure text1 is longer (smaller array size)
step_by_step.step_3: For each row, use 'prev' to track the diagonal value (from row below)
step_by_step.step_4: Before updating dp[j], save its current value in 'temp'
step_by_step.step_5: Update dp[j] using prev (diagonal) and dp[j+1] (right)
step_by_step.step_6: Set prev to temp for the next iteration

explanation.why_it_works: This works because we process from right to left within each row. When we need dp[j+1], it's already been updated for the current row. When we need the diagonal (prev), we save it before overwriting. This cleverly simulates two arrays with just one.
explanation.when_to_use: Use this when you want the absolute minimum space complexity with good cache performance. It's ideal for production systems where memory is at a premium.

prev always holds the diagonal value from the previous row before it gets overwritten
